faqs.question: Who should actually get a Diwali wish with their name and photo on it?
faqs.answer: The eight to ten people whose reaction you would genuinely notice: parents and grandparents, the siblings and cousins you actually talk to, a partner, and the few close friends who live elsewhere. Everyone else on a fifty-name Diwali list is better served by one warm line sent individually, with no graphic at all.

faqs.question: When should I send Diwali wishes in 2026?
faqs.answer: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja) falls on Sunday 8 November 2026, inside the five-day festival that runs 6 to 10 November. Because it is a Sunday, everyone's broadcast messages land in the same few hours, so send the personalised ones on Saturday 7 November or early Sunday morning to be seen at all.

faqs.question: Is a name-on-image JPG or a shareable page better for a Diwali greeting?
faqs.answer: A JPG is the right tool for the broadcast tier because it costs seconds and needs no explanation. A page is worth the twenty minutes only for the few people you want to say something specific to, and it has to work on a phone: 51.8% of the 33,007 views on SubhSandesh pages are mobile (measured 2026-08-19).

faqs.question: Does putting someone's name on a Diwali greeting actually make them appreciate it more?
faqs.answer: Less than senders expect. In Zhang and Epley's 2012 experiments, the effort a giver put in had no measurable effect on how receivers rated the gift (7.22 versus 7.39), while givers confidently predicted it would. The effort paid the giver in felt closeness, not the recipient.

faqs.question: What photo should I use on a Diwali greeting card with a name?
faqs.answer: A photo of your own family or of the two of you, not a stock diya or rangoli. Aknin and Human's six studies found both givers and receivers feel greater closeness from gifts that reflect the giver, which is exactly what a real family photo does and a festival backdrop does not.

faqs.question: Does SubhSandesh have a Diwali template?
faqs.answer: No. There is no Diwali-specific design on SubhSandesh today; the festival templates that exist are Holi and Eid. For Diwali you pick a neutral or romantic layout from the template gallery at https://subhsandesh.in/templates and carry the festival through your own photo and words.

faqs.question: Can I make a free Diwali page for my parents with their name and a family photo?
faqs.answer: Yes, though you will be adapting a non-Diwali layout for now. Pick a simple template from the gallery, use the name they are actually called at home, add one photo they appear in, and publish to get a private link. 99.4% of pages started on SubhSandesh get published and shared (2,722 of 2,739, measured 2026-08-19).

faqs.question: How do I send a personalised Diwali page privately instead of to a group?
faqs.answer: Publish it, then send the link to that one person rather than pasting it into a family group. If it holds photos you do not want forwarded, add a password: 44.3% of SubhSandesh creators do that before sharing (1,213 of 2,739, measured 2026-08-19).

faqs.question: Is it rude to send the same Diwali message to colleagues and clients?
faqs.answer: No, and it is better than the alternative. A colleague does not need their name burned into a diya graphic; what registers is that the message was sent individually rather than forwarded to a list, so write one specific line and send it one at a time.

faqs.question: How many Diwali greetings do people usually send?
faqs.answer: There is no Diwali figure, but Hill and Dunbar's card study is the closest measure: 43 households sent a mean of 68 cards each, ranging from 11 to 149, reaching 153.5 people on average. A Diwali contact list behaves like the upper end of that.

faqs.question: How long does it take to make a Diwali greeting page with a name and photo?
faqs.answer: Twenty to forty minutes for a good one, and it is rarely done in a single sitting. The median SubhSandesh creator leaves 6.9 hours between first save and last edit (sampled on /love-gf, n=914, measured 2026-08-19), so build it on Friday 6 November rather than on Diwali itself.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Wishes With Name and Photo: Who Should Get One

Put a name and photo on a Diwali greeting for the eight or ten people whose reaction you would actually notice, and send everyone else something plain and warm. Diwali is a broadcast festival: the average Christmas-card sender in [Hill and Dunbar's study of 2,984 cards](https://rahill.webspace.durham.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/207/2021/04/Hill-and-Dunbar-2003.pdf) posted 68 cards, and a Diwali list is rarely shorter. Personalised pages behave nothing like that. Across 2,739 pages created on SubhSandesh since 2026-03-12, the average page collects 12.1 views, and 44.3% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it — both measured 2026-08-19. Those are numbers from an artefact made for a handful of people, not a mailing list. This page covers who warrants a named greeting, which photo to use, and when Diwali 2026 lands.

## What a Diwali wish with a name and photo actually is

A Diwali wish with a name and photo is a greeting that carries the recipient's name and at least one photograph, so the message could not have been sent unchanged to anyone else. It exists in two formats: a flat image with the name rendered into the artwork, and a web page with the name, a photo and a message, shared as a link.

The format decides what the recipient can do with it. An image sits in their gallery. A page can hold several photos, a longer message and a password, which 1,213 of 2,739 SubhSandesh creators chose to add before sharing (measured 2026-08-19).

## Diwali is a broadcast festival, so the maths is different

Raksha Bandhan or an anniversary is one-to-one. Diwali is one-to-fifty: parents, siblings, cousins, the school group, four colleagues, two clients, the neighbour, the property dealer who messaged you first. Hill and Dunbar's 43 respondents sent a mean of 68 cards each, with a range from 11 to 149, and the individuals contacted numbered 153.5 on average.

The study's more useful finding for Diwali is what governed contact frequency. Once distance and work relationships were controlled for, **emotional closeness** predicted how often two people were in touch, with the closest ties contacted weekly. Your list is not flat, and the greeting should not be either.

Diwali 2026 sharpens this. Lakshmi Puja falls on **Sunday 8 November 2026**, inside a five-day festival running Friday 6 to Tuesday 10 November. A Sunday means the whole broadcast tier fires at roughly the same hour on a day nobody is at work — exactly when a named greeting is hardest to notice, and the reason to send the personal ones a day early.

## Who on your list actually warrants a name and a photo

Five tiers, in the order we would spend effort on them. Each entry says who it covers, what to personalise, what to skip, and roughly how long it takes.

### 1. Parents and grandparents

The people who will open it twice and show it to someone else. Personalise the name in the form they are actually called — Amma, Papa, Nani — not the name on their Aadhaar card.

Use a photo they appear in, ideally one they have not seen. Skip anything animated that needs a fast connection. Twenty to thirty minutes, and it is the one greeting worth writing from scratch rather than editing.

### 2. Your siblings and the cousins you genuinely talk to

Usually three to six people out of a cousin group of thirty. Personalise with a photo from a shared Diwali, which does the work a written message cannot.

Skip the formal wording; siblings read formality as distance. Ten to fifteen minutes each, and a group page with several photos is legitimate here because the shared history is genuinely shared.

### 3. A partner

The highest-return single greeting on the list, and the one with real product evidence behind it: the ["I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) accounts for 914 of 2,739 pages created and 13,104 of 33,007 recorded views, 39.7% of everything viewed (measured 2026-08-19). Personalise the photo and the message; skip the festival clip-art. Twenty minutes, and Diwali gives you a reason that Valentine's Day has worn out.

### 4. Close friends who live somewhere else

Four or five people, typically the ones distance has quietly downgraded. Personalise the name and one photo of the two of you; that is enough.

Skip trying to summarise the year. Ten minutes each. This tier benefits most from a link rather than an image, because a link survives being reopened in December when the gallery has been cleared.

### 5. Colleagues, clients, neighbours and the wider list

Thirty to forty people, and the honest answer is that none of them need their name on a diya graphic.

Personalise nothing; write one warm, specific, un-forwarded line and send it individually. Skip photos entirely — a photo of your family in a client's WhatsApp is a small imposition. Under a minute each, and the individual send is the entire signal.

## What a name buys you when the recipient knows you sent forty-nine others

Less than most senders assume. In [Zhang and Epley's experiments in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General](https://web2-bschool.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/media_rp/publications/we48l1424841808.pdf) (2012), the effort a giver put into choosing a gift had no measurable effect on how receivers rated it — 7.22 versus 7.39 on their scale, statistically indistinguishable — while givers confidently expected the thoughtful choice to land better. Givers also felt closer to the receiver after choosing thoughtfully (3.70 versus 2.62); receivers felt no difference at all (3.31 versus 3.41).

The mechanism matters for Diwali. Zhang and Epley's argument is that thought only counts when something *triggers* the recipient to consider it. A greeting arriving in a stack of thirty on the same Sunday afternoon is the opposite of a trigger.

This is also where personalisation starts to look automated. [Gino and Flynn's five studies](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/give-them-what-they-want-benefits-explicitness-gift-exchange) (Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, September 2011) found recipients appreciated gifts they had explicitly asked for more than unsolicited ones, while givers assumed both would land equally — givers over-read their own unprompted effort as thoughtful.

A name auto-inserted into forty greeting graphics is unprompted effort of the cheapest kind, and it reads as such. One page for one person reads differently because it visibly could not have been mass-produced.

## Which photo to use, and why a family photo behaves differently

Most name-and-photo generators hand you a diya, a rangoli or a fireworks backdrop and drop the recipient's face into a frame. That inverts what the research suggests works. [SFU's summary of Aknin and Human's six studies](https://www.sfu.ca/fass/news/2017/02/study--giving-a-gift-that-reflects-you-rather-than-your-valentin/) (Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2015) reports that although people prefer to give and receive gifts reflecting the *recipient*, both sides felt greater closeness from gifts that reflected the *giver* — the gift as self-disclosure.

Applied to Diwali: a photo of your own family lighting diyas discloses something. A stock diya discloses nothing, and the recipient's cropped face on festival artwork discloses nothing either.

There is a second trap. [Steffel, Williams and LeBoeuf's working paper](https://marketing.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/Steffel-Williams-LeBoeuf-April-2015.pdf) (April 2015) found givers systematically choose hyper-specific personalised gifts recipients like less: 65% of givers picked a store-specific gift card over a general one against 26% of recipients, and only 18% of givers thought the general card was the more thoughtful choice versus 45% of recipients.

Over-specifying is a giver's instinct, not a recipient's preference. One good photo beats five and a nickname.

## Broadcast greeting versus personal greeting, compared

What each format actually delivers, with SubhSandesh's own measurements in the last column, all taken 2026-08-19.

| Greeting format | What the recipient sees | Effort per recipient | First-party signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forwarded festival image | A graphic they have already received twice | Under 10 seconds | No page created, nothing measurable |
| Name-on-image JPG from a generator | Their name set into stock artwork | 1–2 minutes | No page created, nothing measurable |
| Named page, stock festive photo | Name, message, generic imagery | 10–20 minutes | 12.1 average views per created page |
| Named page, your own family photo | Name, your family, your message | 20–40 minutes; median 6.9 hours between first save and last edit | 99.4% of started pages get published (2,722 of 2,739) |
| Named page with a password | A page that needs a shared password | Adds about a minute | 44.3% of creators add one (1,213 of 2,739) |

The takeaway: effort scales with the format, and 51.8% of the 33,007 views recorded on shared pages happen on a phone (17,101 views), so whatever you build has to survive a 6-inch screen first.

## When a name and photo is the wrong choice

Three cases, said plainly. If the recipient has no smartphone, a link is worse than a printed card and a phone call — 51.8% of views being mobile is a fact about the medium, not an argument for it.

If you are in the same house on 8 November, a greeting page is a strange substitute for saying शुभ दीपावली (*Shubh Deepavali*, "auspicious Diwali") over the diyas. And if a photo would embarrass the recipient in a work group, the plain line wins.

The product limit is worth stating too: SubhSandesh has **no Diwali template today**. The festival designs that exist are Holi and Eid, and the nearest festive-styled option is the [Holi greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/holi), which is visibly a Holi design.

For Diwali right now, the honest route is a neutral or romantic layout from the [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates), with the Diwali feeling supplied by your own photo and words. If a Diwali-specific design matters more than a personal photo, use a card builder instead.

The median creator keeps editing for 6.9 hours between first save and last edit (sampled on /love-gf, n=914, measured 2026-08-19). Build yours on Friday 6 November, so the Sunday is a send and not a build.

J., "Give a piece of you: Gifts that reflect givers promote closeness", *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology*, 2015 — [university summary, Simon Fraser University, 14 February 2017](https://www.sfu.ca/fass/news/2017/02/study--giving-a-gift-that-reflects-you-rather-than-your-valentin/)

failed.why: The 123-word opening answer paragraph runs six sentences on purpose, so an answer engine can lift one self-contained block containing the direct answer plus three first-party numbers. Every other paragraph in the body is one to three sentences; splitting the opener would cost the extractable answer.

The claim that a Diwali list runs to dozens rests on Hill and Dunbar's British Christmas-card data, which is the closest measured proxy rather than Indian evidence.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this query that tells a reader to personalise fewer greetings, and it backs that with measured card-sending volumes, giver-versus-recipient experiments the retailers and generators never touch, and first-party numbers (12.1 views per page, 44.3% password rate) nobody else can print. The weakness is that none of the first-party facts are Diwali-specific — Diwali is not one of the 13 page types, and the platform-wide figures would fit any post in this batch, so they support the argument without being unique to it. Domain authority is far below the name-on-image generators that own this SERP, and there is no Diwali template to convert the traffic, so treat this as a months-long play, not a ranking prediction.
